items.d: An introduction to the WidgetCore plugin for Elementor — accessible widgets: an FAQ accordion with FAQPage schema, an AJAX live search and a comments widget, with requirements and a reading path.
h: What the plugin does not do
items.b: WidgetCore is a free, open-source WordPress plugin that adds a growing set of practical, ready-to-use widgets to Elementor — including an accessible FAQ accordion that outputs FAQPage structured data, a live search that shows results without reloading the page, also available anywhere on the site through the [wgcr_search] shortcode, and a comments widget with a list and a configurable form ([wgcr_comments]). Every widget the plugin ships has its own guide page in these docs, and the set grows with each release. The plugin focuses on three things: real accessibility (keyboard support, ARIA and reduced motion), first-class Persian and right-to-left support (with fa_IR and en_US translations bundled), and staying light (no external JavaScript or CSS library, no requests of its own beyond the update check). The widgets FAQ widgetEvery content and style control, keyboard behaviour and the structured data output.Comments widgetThe comment list and the comment form with full control over fields, layout and style; with a shortcode and no extra plugin.Live Search widgetGeneral, Layout, Query and Pagination sections plus the style sections, in two display modes.Tabs widgetHorizontal or vertical tabs with full accessibility, keyboard navigation and optional row wrapping.Counter widgetAn animated number with prefix and suffix that runs once when scrolled into view — and shows the final num

Step 1 — Install the plugin Download widgetcore.zip from the download page and upload it under “Plugins → Add New → Upload Plugin” in the WordPress dashboard, then click Activate. items.d: The mental model behind WidgetCore — display mode, source and query, Elementor templates, pagination, widget identifiers and the root classes that every setting maps onto.
items.b: The plugin has few controls, but they all rest on a handful of simple concepts. Once you know them, the rest of the documentation reads fast. Widgets, instances and identifiers Every time you place a widget you create an instance with a unique identifier. In the live search widget that identifier becomes the root element's DOM id: php $uid = 'wgcr-search-' . sanitize_html_class( $uid !== '' ? $uid : 'sc' . $counter ); So two search widgets on the same page each keep their own root, state and results, and never interfere with each other. In the FAQ widget, each item's identifier combines the widget id and the item index (wgcr-faq-q-{uid} and wgcr-faq-a-{uid}), which keeps aria-controls and aria-labelledby unique. Display modes The live search has two display modes, and this choice determines how the rest of the controls behave: Mode Control value Where results appear Available controls List mode modal A dropdown panel below the field; closes on outside click General, Layout, Query, Pagination Page mode page An always-visible region inside the same widget Plus columns, masonry, equal height and container styling Display modes pageA full comparison of the two modes with example configurations. Source and query The source (source) is the post type that gets searched. Only public, searchable post types are allowed; an invalid value falls back to post: php function wgcr_searc

items.d: Step-by-step installation of WidgetCore in WordPress using three methods (ZIP upload, FTP and WP-CLI), activation, verifying the widgets in Elementor and removing the plugin.
h: Method 2 — Manual copy over FTP or a file manager
items.b: Installing the plugin is exactly like installing any other WordPress plugin. This page covers three methods, how to verify the result and what deleting the plugin does. Method 1 — Upload from the dashboard (recommended) Download the package Get widgetcore.zip from the download page. Do not unzip it. Go to the plugins screen In the WordPress dashboard: “Plugins → Add New”, then the “Upload Plugin” button at the top. Choose the file and install Select the ZIP file and click “Install Now”. Activate After the install finishes, click “Activate Plugin”. Method 2 — Manual copy over FTP or a file manager Unzip the package You get a widgetcore/ folder. Put the folder in wp-content/plugins/ The final path must be wp-content/plugins/widgetcore/widgetcore.php. Activate the plugin Click “Activate” on the Plugins screen. A common manual-install mistake If the path ends up as wp-content/plugins/widgetcore/widgetcore/widgetcore.php, the plugin will not appear in the list. Remove one folder level so that widgetcore.php sits directly inside widgetcore/. Method 3 — WP-CLI bash wp plugin install "https://github.com/WidgetCore/Plugin/releases/latest/download/widgetcore.zip" --activate If Elementor is installed but inactive, activate it as well: bash wp plugin activate elementor wp plugin list --status=active --fields=name,version,update_version What activation changes Event Hook Result Wi

items.d: Updating WidgetCore straight from the GitHub repository — the check-for-updates link, native auto-updates, release notes, an optional token and switching back to WordPress.org.
items.b: From version 0.1.2 onwards the plugin receives new releases directly from the GitHub repository. This is done with the Update URI header and WordPress core hooks only — no update library is installed. Updates at a glance WordPress asks GitHub for the published release Every update check reads the latest release of the WidgetCore/Plugin repository. A newer version shows up in the plugins list With the usual WordPress notice: “A new version is available”. Update with one click The widgetcore.zip asset of that release is downloaded and replaces the plugin. Read the release notes On the “View details” screen, the changelog section is filled from the release body. The “Check for updates” link Under the WidgetCore row on “Plugins” there is a link called Check for updates (visible only to users with the update_plugins capability). Clicking it: Clears the plugin cache (wp_clean_plugins_cache( true )). Runs the update check immediately (wp_update_plugins()). Shows a notice with the result: either that a new version is available, or that you are on the latest one. Why the link exists WordPress checks for updates every 12 hours by default. If a release was published just now, you may not see it until the next scheduled check without this link. items.b: The Comments widget shows the current post's comment list and the comment form in one widget. Saving, spam checks, manual approval and notification emails stay the job of WordPress itself; the widget only gives you control over the look, the layout and the form fields. It needs no other plugin, ships no JavaScript of its own and creates no page or option in the dashboard. Set the look In the Style tab change the colours, borders, spacing and typography of each part. h: Check that the REST API works
items.b: WidgetCore has exactly one REST route: the one the Live Search widget and the [wgcr_search] shortcode use to fetch results. It is public and documented, so you can call it from your own JavaScript, a mobile app or another plugin. This page lists every route and the rules they share. A route that needs a longer explanation has its own page under this one. All REST routes Route Method Used by Access Complete reference /wp-json/wgcr/v1/search GET Live Search widget, [wgcr_search] Public (no login, no nonce) The search REST endpoint The Comments and FAQ widgets have no REST route. See Features that use no REST below. Rules they share Namespace: every WidgetCore route lives under wgcr/v1. The full address is https://example.com/wp-json/wgcr/v1/<route>; without pretty permalinks, use https://example.com/?rest_route=/wgcr/v1/<route>. Read only: the routes answer GET and return JSON. Nothing is written to the database, no option, cookie or meta is created. Public data only: results contain only what any visitor can already reach, such as published posts without a password. Custom filters on your site can change this, so keep them safe. Errors follow WordPress: a failed request returns the standard REST error object with code, message and data.status. items.d: The WidgetCore search REST endpoint — the route, every parameter with its type and default, the response shape, pagination headers, request examples and the status codes.
items.b: The search widget and the shortcode both talk to a single REST endpoint. You can call it yourself from JavaScript, from a mobile app or from another plugin. The endpoint Item Value Namespace wgcr/v1 Route /search Full address https://example.com/wp-json/wgcr/v1/search Method GET Permission callback __return_true (public) Result cap WGCR_SEARCH_MAX_RESULTS (50) Why the route is public Search results only ever contain published posts without passwords, which any visitor can already reach through the theme's search page. Making the route public removes the need for nonces and lets you use the endpoint from any client. These are the default query guarantees. Custom wgcr_search_query_args filters run after the base arguments are built and can change them: preserve post_status => publish, has_password => false, public searchable post types and sensible limits. The public route does not reapply those constraints after filters. items.d: How WidgetCore meets accessibility requirements — the combobox pattern, ARIA roles, live regions, working without JavaScript, FAQ semantics, reduced motion, contrast and an audit checklist.
items.b: Accessibility in this plugin is not an extra layer: the markup, the keyboard behaviour and the ARIA attributes are built into every widget from the start. This page explains what is already handled and what you should check when you customise the output. Live Search widget The combobox pattern The field follows the WAI-ARIA combobox pattern: Element Attribute Meaning The input role="combobox" Announced as a combined field and list The input aria-expanded="true/false" Whether the results panel is open The input aria-controls="…-list" The id of the results list The input aria-autocomplete="list" Suggestions come from a list The input aria-activedescendant="…" The currently highlighted result The results list role="listbox" A selectable list Each result role="option" A selectable item The selected result aria-selected="true" The highlighted option Label and accessible name Every field has an accessible name: a visible <label> when there is room, otherwise aria-label. The panel has aria-label too, and the results list is associated with the field through aria-controls. Do not remove the label If you restyle the field and hide the label with display: none, replace it with an accessible alternative such as aria-label or a visually-hidden label class. items.b: Every widget can be used entirely from the keyboard. This page lists every binding, in the widget and on this documentation site, plus the test patterns we recommend. Live Search widget When focus is on the field Key Behaviour Typing (2 or more characters) Sends a debounced request (250 ms) and opens the results panel ArrowDown Highlights the first result, or the next one; wraps from last to first ArrowUp Highlights the previous result, or the last one when at the top Enter Opens the highlighted result; with nothing highlighted, submits the form Escape List mode: closes an open panel; if already closed, clears the query. Page mode: clears the query immediately The highlighted result is tracked with aria-activedescendant on the field, so a screen reader announces the option as you move through the list without moving DOM focus. Enter without a highlight When no result is highlighted, Enter performs the form's default submit and the visitor goes to the site's search results page. This is intentional: the field behaves like a normal search form. When focus is inside the results Key Behaviour Tab Moves through the focusable elements of each result (links) Enter Activates the focused link Arrow and Escape handlers apply to the input, not to links inside results. h: Building a translation for a new language
items.b: The plugin ships complete Persian and English translations and a POT template for any other language. All interface texts come from these files — nothing is hardcoded in the output. Language files File Language Status languages/widgetcore-fa_IR.mo / .po Persian Complete, bundled languages/widgetcore-en_US.mo / .po English Complete, bundled languages/widgetcore.pot Template For building a new translation Translations are loaded on init at priority 1: php function wgcr_load_translations() { $domain = 'widgetcore'; $locale = determine_locale(); $global = WP_LANG_DIR . '/plugins/' . $domain . '-' . $locale . '.mo'; if ( is_readable( $global ) ) { load_textdomain( $domain, $global, $locale ); } load_textdomain( $domain, WGCR_DIR . 'languages/' . $domain . '-' . $locale . '.mo', $locale ); } Load order The plugin resolves the current locale with determine_locale() and calls load_textdomain for the readable global file first, then the bundled file. The first-loaded translation wins for shared strings; missing strings fall back to the bundled catalog: Priority Path Notes 1 wp-content/languages/plugins/widgetcore-{locale}.mo The global directory — your file wins here 2 wp-content/plugins/widgetcore/languages/widgetcore-{locale}.mo The bundled translation Overriding a single string To change one wording without editing the plugin, copy the bundled .po for your locale into wp-content/lang

items.b: The questions that come up most often. If yours is not answered here, see the troubleshooting page. Is the plugin free? Yes. WidgetCore is free and open source under the GPL-2.0-or-later license, the same license as WordPress itself. There is no paid version, no licence key and no feature that unlocks later. You can use it on as many sites as you like, and you can modify it. What does the plugin require? Requirement Minimum WordPress 6.7 PHP 7.4 Elementor Installed and active Elementor tested up to 4.3.4 Elementor is a hard requirement: every widget extends Elementor's Widget_Base class, so without Elementor no widget is registered. The verified compatibility matrix is on the requirements page. Does the plugin work on left-to-right sites? Yes. All layout rules use logical properties (inset-inline-start, margin-inline, text-align: start), so the widgets follow the document direction automatically. On an English (LTR) site the icon sits on the right side of the field and the panel aligns to the left; on a Persian (RTL) site everything mirrors. There is a single stylesheet and no separate RTL file. I cannot find the widgets in the Elementor editor. What should I do? items.d: Ways to contribute to the open source WidgetCore plugin — from bug reports and feedback to documentation improvements, translations and code.
items.b: WidgetCore is an open source plugin under the GPL license, and it grows with help from its community. You do not have to be a programmer to contribute; precise, well-documented feedback is just as valuable. Reporting a bug Start with the troubleshooting page — many common problems are already solved there. If the problem remains: Open an issue in the plugin repository on GitHub: WidgetCore/Plugin. Include your WordPress, Elementor, PHP and plugin versions (all explained on the requirements page). Describe what you expected and what happened instead; if you can, list the steps that reproduce the problem. Keep one problem per report so it stays easy to track. Suggesting improvements Share ideas for new widgets, new controls or better documentation through the issue tracker. Before suggesting, check the FAQ and the widget guides — what you need may already exist and only needs to be found. Documentation and translation If you spot an error, a gap or a confusing sentence anywhere in these docs, report it. Fixing text and translating the documentation into other languages is one of the most valuable contributions, because it helps every user get the plugin right. Contributing code If you write PHP or JavaScript: For anything beyond a small fix, open an issue first so we can agree on the scope.
